lessons.title: Overview of Bladesmithing History and Traditions
lessons.body: Bladesmithing in Africa goes back over 2,000 years. The Haya people of Tanzania were smelting high-carbon steel in preheated forced-draft furnaces around 500 BCE, producing tools and weapons. In West Africa, the Nok culture (500 BCEâ200 CE) made iron blades, and later the Benin Kingdom (13thâ19th century) had specialized blacksmith guilds that forged ceremonial swords and practical knives. The Zulu under Shaka Zulu (early 19th century) used short stabbing spears called iklwa, forged from locally smelted iron. These traditions were not primitiveâthey involved sophisticated heat treatment and alloying. For example, Haya smiths preheated their furnaces with charcoal to reach 1,800Â°C, producing carbon steel with 0.5â1.5% carbon. Today, modern African bladesmiths blend these techniques with imported tools. In Nigeria, the Nupe people still forge knives from recycled car springs. In Kenya, the Maasai make swords from leaf springs of trucks. Your work continues this lineage. Start by studying local smiths: visit a nearby forge, ask about their steel sources (often scrap: machetes, car parts, railroad clips). Note their quenching methodsâsome use used motor oil, others use water from specific rivers. Document what you see. This history matters because it shows bladesmithing is not foreign; it is indigenous. You are not copying Europe; you are reviving and upgrading African metallurgy. Your first practical step: find three different locally made knives or tools. Examine their edges, tangs, and handles. Ask the makers how they were made. That is your baseline. From there, you will learn to make better blades using both traditional wisdom and modern safety.

lessons.title: Essential Tools and Equipment for the Bladesmith
lessons.body: You need six core tools to start bladesmithing: a forge, an anvil, a hammer, tongs, a quench tank, and a file. In Africa, you can build or source these locally. Forge: a simple ground forge made from a hole in the ground, a clay-lined bucket, or a car brake drum. Use charcoal or coal as fuel. Add a tuyere (a pipe) connected to a hand-cranked blower or bellowsâa hair dryer on cool setting works if you have electricity. Anvil: a 20â50 kg piece of railroad track, a large sledgehammer head, or a block of hardened steel. Mount it at knuckle height (about 70 cm for most adults). Hammer: a 1â1.5 kg cross-peen or ball-peen hammer. Start with one hammer; add a 2 kg sledge for striking. Tongs: flat-jaw tongs for holding hot steel. You can make them from 6 mm round bar or buy used ones. Quench tank: a metal bucket or PVC pipe filled with 20 liters of water, used motor oil, or brine (1 kg salt per 10 liters water). File: a 10â12 inch bastard file for shaping and sharpening. Also get: safety glasses (essential), leather gloves, ear plugs, and a leather apron. For measuring, a simple tape measure and a center punch. For cutting, a hacksaw or angle grinder with cutting disc. Total cost in most African cities: $50â$150 if you scavenge. Where to find: scrapyards for railroad track and car springs; hardware stores for files and hammers; market welders for tongs. Set up a dedicated workspaceâat least 3x3 meters, with a dirt or concrete floor, away from flammable materials. Do not forge in a closed room; carbon monoxide kills. Your first project: make a simple poker from 10 mm mild steel rod. This teaches fire management, hammer control, and quenching.

lessons.title: Understanding Steel Types and Their Properties
lessons.body: Steel is iron mixed with 0.2% to 2.1% carbon. More carbon means harder but more brittle. For blades, you want 0.5% to 1.0% carbon. Low-carbon steel (mild steel, 0.1â0.3% carbon) is easy to forge but won't hold an edge. High-carbon steel (0.6â1.0% carbon) is ideal for knives. In Africa, your best sources of high-carbon steel are: car and truck leaf springs (5160 steel, 0.5â0.6% carbon), coil springs (1080 steel, 0.8% carbon), railroad clips (1060 steel), and old files (1095 steel, 0.9â1.0% carbon). Avoid galvanized steel (zinc coating is toxic when heated), stainless steel (hard to forge and heat treat without precise temperatures), and cast iron (too brittle). Test steel with a grinder: sparks from high-carbon steel are short, bright, and burst close to the wheel; low-carbon sparks are long, yellow, and go far. A file test: a new file will skate on hardened high-carbon steel but bite into mild steel. Heat treatment: heat steel to non-magnetic (about 770Â°Câcherry red in dim light), then quench in oil (for springs and files) or water (for 1095). Temper immediately: clean the blade, heat to 200Â°C for 1 hour (straw yellow color) for a knife edge. This relieves stress and prevents cracking. In Africa, many smiths use charcoal fires and judge temperature by color: dark red (550Â°C), cherry red (770Â°C), orange (900Â°C), yellow (1100Â°C). Practice with a magnetâwhen steel stops being magnetic, it's ready to quench. Start with leaf spring steel. It is forgiving, cheap, and abundant. Forge one knife from a 20 cm piece of leaf spring. Normalize it (heat to non-magnetic and air cool) three times before quenching to refine grain. That is your foundation.

lessons.title: Workshop Safety and Protective Gear
lessons.body: Bladesmithing can kill you or maim you if you ignore safety. The four biggest dangers: burns, cuts, eye injuries, and toxic fumes. Protect yourself with gear that costs less than $30 total. Eye protection: wear safety glasses or a face shield at all times. Hot scale (iron oxide flakes) flies off when you hammer. Grinding sparks can blind you. Gloves: thick leather gloves for holding tongs and hot metal. Never wear synthetic glovesâthey melt. Ear protection: forging is loud (100â110 dB). Use foam earplugs or earmuffs. Apron: leather apron protects your torso from burns and cuts. Boots: closed leather boots, not sandals. Clothing: cotton or wool, long sleeves, no loose ends. Fire safety: keep a bucket of water and a bucket of sand within arm's reach. Never forge near gasoline, paint, or dry grass. Forge outside or in a well-ventilated shed with open doors. Carbon monoxide from charcoal is odorless and deadlyânever forge in a closed room. Quenching safety: hot oil can flash into flames. Keep a lid nearby to smother oil fires. Never quench in water after oil without cleaning the bladeâwater can explode into steam. Toxic metals: avoid galvanized steel (zinc fumes cause metal fume fever), lead, and cadmium. If you must grind or weld unknown steel, wear a respirator (N95 or better). First aid: keep a burn kit with clean cloths, antibiotic ointment, and pain relievers. For minor burns, cool with running water for 10 minutes, then cover. For cuts, apply pressure and seek medical help if deep. Hammer safety: check your hammer head for cracks; a loose head can fly off. Dress your hammer face smoothâa chipped face can send shrapnel. Finally, work sober and rested. Fatigue causes mistakes. Set up your forge so you never have to reach over the fire. Your safety habits will keep you bladesmithing for decades.

lessons.title: Setting Up Your Forge and Anvil
lessons.body: A functional forge needs three things: a fire pit, air blast, and fuel. Build a simple ground forge: dig a hole 30 cm wide and 15 cm deep. Line it with clay or a mixture of clay and sand. Insert a 1.5 cm iron pipe (tuyere) at a 20-degree angle, with the end 5 cm above the bottom. Connect the pipe to a blowerâa hand-cranked blower from a scrapyard, a bellows made from a tire inner tube, or a hair dryer on cool. For fuel, use charcoal (hardwood charcoal burns hotter and cleaner than softwood) or coal. Do not use charcoal briquettesâthey contain additives. For an anvil, mount a 30â50 cm piece of railroad track vertically in a log or bucket of concrete, with the top at knuckle height (70 cm). If you have a real anvil, place it on a stump and secure it with chains or nails. The horn (pointed end) is for bending; the face is for flattening; the hardy hole (square hole) holds tools. If no anvil, a large sledgehammer head or a thick steel plate works. Set your forge and anvil 1 meter apartâclose enough to move hot steel quickly, far enough to avoid bumping. Add a quench tank (bucket of oil) 1 meter from the anvil. Add a water bucket for cooling tongs and hands. Lighting the forge: place paper and kindling in the pit, add charcoal, and gently blow air. Once lit, add more charcoal around the sides, leaving a hollow in the center for the steel. You want a fire 10â15 cm deep. Air control: more air = hotter fire. Learn to adjust your blower. A good forging fire reaches 1,200â1,400Â°C. Test with a piece of mild steelâit should become bright orange in 2â3 minutes. Keep your forge clean: remove clinker (fused ash) with a poker. In Africa, many smiths use a simple clay forge with a goatskin bellows. That works. Start there. Upgrade later.

lessons.title: Basic Forging Techniques: Tapering, Drawing, and Upsetting
lessons.body: Three fundamental forging techniques: tapering, drawing, and upsetting. Tapering: making a point or reducing thickness at one end. Heat the end of your steel to bright orange (900â1,000Â°C). Place it on the anvil with the hot end over the edge. Strike with your hammer at a slight angle, turning the steel 90 degrees every few hits. For a knife tang, taper from 6 mm to 3 mm over 10 cm. Draw the taper outâdon't just squash it. Drawing: lengthening steel by reducing its cross-section. Heat a 5 cm section to orange. Hammer from the center outward, using the hammer's face. Turn the steel 90 degrees and repeat. Each heat should lengthen the steel by 1â2 cm. For a knife blade, draw a 10 cm piece of leaf spring to 15 cm, reducing thickness from 6 mm to 4 mm. Use the horn of the anvil for curved draws. Upsetting: thickening steel by hammering on its end. Heat the end to orange, stand it vertically on the anvil, and strike the top with a hammer. This shortens and thickens the steel. Use upsetting to create a bolster or to thicken a tang. For a knife, upset the first 2 cm of the tang to 8 mm thick. Critical rules: always forge at the right temperatureâtoo cold (below 800Â°C, dark red) causes cracks; too hot (above 1,200Â°C, sparking) burns the steel. Never hammer cold steel. Use light blows for precision, heavy blows for moving metal. Keep your hammer face polished. Practice each technique on mild steel first. Make three tapering exercises: a 20 cm rod tapered to a point, a flat taper (like a screwdriver), and a round taper. Then draw a 10 cm square bar to 20 cm. Then upset a 10 cm bar to 8 cm. Do this until you can control the shape. In Africa, smiths often use a heavy stone as an anvil and a simple hammer. The technique is the same. Your first knife: take a 20 cm piece of leaf spring, draw a 10 cm blade, taper the tang, and upset the tang end. That is your module project.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Bladesmithing in the African Context

This practical reference distils the six lessons of the Introduction to Bladesmithing module into a working document you can keep at the forge. It is written for the African bladesmith who is building a business, not just a hobby: every table, diagram and checklist below is designed to help you make better blades, waste less steel, keep your workshop safe and price your work profitably.

Bladesmithing has deep roots across the continent. From the iron-smelting furnaces of the Haya people in Tanzania to the blacksmith guilds of the Sahel and the knife-making traditions of North Africa, African smiths have shaped tools, weapons and trade goods for over two millennia. Today, the market for hand-forged knives, machetes, agricultural blades and custom cutlery is growing â driven by tourism, culinary tourism, bushcraft culture and a renewed interest in heritage craft. The smith who understands steel, heat and safety has a genuine business opportunity.

Understanding Steel: The Foundation of Every Blade

Steel is iron with a controlled amount of carbon, usually between 0.05% and 2.0%. The carbon content determines hardness, toughness and edge retention. For bladesmithing, the useful range is roughly 0.5% to 1.2% carbon. Below that, the blade will not hold an edge; above it, the steel becomes brittle and difficult to forge without cracking.

In many African workshops, smiths work with recycled steel: leaf springs from vehicles, coil springs, ball bearings, files, and railway clips. These are excellent sources of medium- to high-carbon steel, but their composition is inconsistent. The table below gives practical guidance on common African scrap sources.

Table 1: Common recycled steel sources in African workshops and their suitability for blades
Source Typical carbon content Best use Notes
Vehicle leaf spring 0.50â0.70% Machetes, heavy choppers, agricultural blades Tough, forgiving to forge; may contain micro-cracks from fatigue
Coil spring 0.55â0.75% Knives, swords, drawknives Often cleaner than leaf springs; check for pitting
Ball bearing / bearing race 0.90â1.10% Small knives, chisels, punches High carbon; requires careful forging and normalising
Metal file 1.00â1.20% Fine cutting tools, small knives Hard and brittle; forge at lower temperature to avoid cracking
Railway clip / fishplate 0.60â0.80% Heavy blades, axes, tools Abundant in many regions; can be tough to move under the hammer
Mild steel (construction bar) 0.10â0.20% Fittings, guards, decorative work Not suitable for cutting edges

Source: Adapted from Verhoeven, J.D. (2007) Steel Metallurgy for the Non-Metallurgist, ASM International; and practical workshop data from African bladesmith training programmes.

Heat Treatment: Where the Blade Is Made or Broken

Forging shapes the blade; heat treatment gives it its soul. The three critical stages are normalising, hardening and tempering. In an African workshop without a thermocouple, you must learn to read colour. The table below converts colour to temperature and action.

Table 2: Steel colour, approximate temperature and recommended action
Colour Approx. temperature (Â°C) Action
Faint red (first visible) 540â600 Too cold to forge; steel may crack
Dark cherry red 650â700 Normalising range for medium-carbon steel
Cherry red 750â800 Forging range begins; good for drawing and tapering
Bright orange 850â900 Ideal forging range for most blade steels
Yellow 950â1000 Hardening range for many simple carbon steels
White / sparkling 1100+ Too hot; grain growth and burning risk

Source: Adapted from Verhoeven, J.D. (2007) Steel Metallurgy for the Non-Metallurgist, ASM International; and the Heat Treater's Guide: Practices and Procedures for Irons and Steels (ASM International).

For hardening, heat the blade to non-magnetic (approximately 760â800Â°C for simple carbon steels), then quench in the appropriate medium â warm oil for most blade steels, brine or water only for shallow-hardening steels. Temper immediately at 180â220Â°C for one hour, twice, to relieve stress and reduce brittleness. Skip the temper and your blade will snap in the customer's hand.

â  SAFETY WARNING â QUENCHING AND FIRE RISK

Quenching oil can flash into flame when a hot blade is plunged into it. Always:

  • Quench in a metal container with a lid nearby to smother flames.
  • Never quench near dry grass, thatch, fuel drums or gas cylinders â a common hazard in African workshops.
  • Wear a leather apron, face shield and gloves. Hot oil splashes cause severe burns.
  • Keep a dry-powder fire extinguisher or sand bucket within arm's reach.
  • Work outdoors or in a well-ventilated area; quenching oil fumes are toxic.

If a quench fire starts, do not use water on an oil fire. Cover the container with its lid or smother with sand.

Business-First Notes for the African Bladesmith

Your forge is a business asset. Three practical points:

  • Price for profit, not for praise. Calculate the cost of steel, fuel (charcoal, coke or gas), abrasives, electricity and your time. A hand-forged knife that takes eight hours and sells for the price of a factory blade is a hobby, not a business. Aim for a minimum 3Ã material cost plus a fair hourly rate.
  • Standardise your best sellers. Identify the three blades that sell most â often a bush knife, a kitchen knife and a small utility knife â and make them in batches. Batch production reduces fuel consumption per blade and improves consistency.
  • Document your steel. Keep a notebook recording the source of every piece of steel, its forging behaviour and its heat-treatment results. Over time this becomes your most valuable business asset: a tested, repeatable material library.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Steel identified? Know the carbon content and source before you strike. Test with a spark test or a file if unsure.
  2. Forge at the right colour? Bright orange (850â900Â°C) for most forging; never forge below cherry red.
  3. Anvil secure? Check the stump and anvil are stable and at the correct height â knuckles of a closed fist should just touch the anvil face.
  4. Safety gear on? Leather apron, gloves, eye protection, closed leather boots, hearing protection if grinding.
  5. Quench ready? Correct medium (warm oil for most steels), correct temperature, lid and extinguisher within reach.
  6. Normalise before hardening? Three normalising cycles refine grain and prevent warping or cracking.
  7. Temper twice? 180â220Â°C for one hour, twice, immediately after hardening.
  8. Record the result? Note steel source, heat treatment and final performance in your workshop logbook.

Further Reading

  • Project Gutenberg â Historical works on blacksmithing and metalwork (free public-domain texts on traditional forging).
  • Internet Archive â Steel Metallurgy for the Non-Metallurgist (Verhoeven) (borrowable reference on steel structure and heat treatment).
  • NIST â Materials measurement and standards resources (free technical data on metals and testing).
  • South African Bureau of Standards (SABS) (free catalogue of standards relevant to tools and metal products).
  • Smithsonian National Museum of African Art â African metalwork and blacksmithing traditions (free online collections and context).

Final word: Bladesmithing in Africa is not a curiosity â it is a trade with a market. The smith who combines traditional skill with modern understanding of steel, heat treatment and safety, and who runs the forge as a business, will outlast the smith who treats it as a pastime. Master the basics in this module, keep this reference at your anvil, and build a reputation one blade at a time.

quiz.q: Which African culture was smelting high-carbon steel around 500 BCE?
options: B) The Zulu of South Africa
quiz.explanation: The Haya people of Tanzania developed a preheated forced-draft furnace that produced high-carbon steel around 500 BCE.

quiz.q: What is the ideal carbon content for a knife blade?
quiz.explanation: 0.5â1.0% carbon provides a balance of hardness and toughness suitable for knives.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good source of high-carbon steel in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Car leaf springs are typically made from 5160 steel with 0.5â0.6% carbon, ideal for blades.

quiz.q: What is the first thing you should do if you get a minor burn?
options: B) Cool with running water for 10 minutes
D) Wrap tightly with a bandage
quiz.explanation: Cooling with water reduces tissue damage and pain; other methods can worsen the burn.

quiz.q: How high should your anvil be mounted?
quiz.explanation: Knuckle height allows for proper hammer swing and control without fatigue.

quiz.q: What is the correct order of steps for heat treating a knife?
quiz.explanation: Normalizing refines grain, quenching hardens, and tempering reduces brittleness.

quiz.q: Which fuel should you avoid in a forge?
quiz.explanation: Charcoal briquettes contain additives that can produce toxic fumes and inconsistent heat.

quiz.q: What is the main danger of forging galvanized steel?
options: A) It is too hard to forge
B) It produces toxic zinc fumes
quiz.explanation: Zinc coating vaporizes at forging temperatures and causes metal fume fever when inhaled.

quiz.q: What does a short, bright spark from a grinder indicate?
quiz.explanation: High-carbon steel produces short, bright sparks that burst close to the grinding wheel.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of normalizing steel?
options: B) To soften it for filing
quiz.explanation: Normalizing relieves internal stresses and refines grain, improving toughness.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to hold hot steel?
quiz.explanation: Tongs are designed to securely hold hot metal during forging.

quiz.q: What is the approximate temperature of cherry red steel?
quiz.explanation: Cherry red corresponds to about 770Â°C, the non-magnetic point for steel.

quiz.q: Why should you never forge in a closed room?
options: B) Carbon monoxide can build up
C) The fire needs more oxygen
quiz.explanation: Charcoal fires produce carbon monoxide, an odorless gas that can be fatal in enclosed spaces.

quiz.q: What is upsetting in forging?
options: B) Thickening steel by hammering its end
quiz.explanation: Upsetting increases the cross-section by compressing the end of a heated bar.

quiz.q: Which of these is a safe practice when quenching in oil?
options: B) Keep a lid nearby to smother flames
C) Use gasoline as quench oil
D) Quench in a plastic bucket
quiz.explanation: Hot oil can ignite; a lid smothers flames safely.

quiz.q: What is the best source of an anvil if you cannot buy one?
options: B) A piece of railroad track
quiz.explanation: Railroad track is hard, heavy, and can be mounted to serve as an anvil.

quiz.q: What is the correct hammer weight for most forging?
quiz.explanation: A 1â1.5 kg hammer provides enough force for control and efficiency.

quiz.q: What does drawing out mean in bladesmithing?
options: B) Lengthening steel by reducing its cross-section
quiz.explanation: Drawing increases length while decreasing thickness or width.

quiz.q: Which steel is best for a beginner?
quiz.explanation: Leaf spring steel is forgiving, abundant, and has good carbon content.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a tuyere in a forge?
options: B) To deliver air to the fire
quiz.explanation: The tuyere is a pipe that directs air into the fire to increase heat.

quiz.q: How often should you turn the steel when tapering?
quiz.explanation: Turning frequently ensures an even taper and prevents flat spots.

quiz.q: What color should steel be before quenching?
quiz.explanation: Cherry red (about 770Â°C) is the correct quenching temperature for most simple steels.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a recommended protective gear?
quiz.explanation: Synthetic gloves can melt and stick to skin when exposed to hot metal.

quiz.q: What is the first step in building a ground forge?
options: A) Dig a hole and line with clay
quiz.explanation: The fire pit must be prepared before adding fuel and lighting.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of charcoal over coal?
options: B) It is cleaner and produces less smoke
quiz.explanation: Charcoal burns cleaner with less sulfur and smoke, though coal can be hotter.

quiz.q: What is the correct tempering temperature for a knife edge?
quiz.explanation: Tempering at 200Â°C for one hour produces a straw-yellow color, ideal for knife edges.

quiz.q: Which African people are known for forging the iklwa spear?
quiz.explanation: The Zulu under Shaka Zulu used the iklwa, a short stabbing spear.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a hardy hole in an anvil?
options: B) To hold tools like chisels
quiz.explanation: The hardy hole is a square hole that secures bottom tools.

quiz.q: What should you do if your hammer head is loose?
options: B) Tighten or replace the handle
quiz.explanation: A loose hammer head can fly off and cause serious injury.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to test if steel is non-magnetic?
options: B) Hit it with a hammer
quiz.explanation: A magnet will not stick to steel above its Curie temperature (about 770Â°C).
